summary.text: Abyssal plains are flat, smooth stretches of deep ocean floor, usually lying 3,000 to 6,000 metres down.
They form when fine clay and silt, much of it carried by turbidity currents down submarine canyons, blanket the uneven crust made by seafloor spreading.
They cover more than half of Earth's surface, yet darkness and water pressure of up to about 750 times atmospheric pressure leave them poorly explored.

facts.label: Metals in nodules
facts.value: Manganese, iron, nickel, cobalt and copper

items.prompt: Counting land and sea together, roughly how much of Earth's whole surface do abyssal plains cover?
items.explain: Abyssal plains cover more than 50% of Earth's surface.

items.prompt: The ocean crust under an abyssal plain is bumpy, yet the plain on top is very smooth. Why?

options.label: Fine sediment has settled over the bumps
Deep currents have ground the rock flat
Lava spread out and cooled in a flat sheet
Old ice sheets scraped the bottom level

items.explain: Abyssal plains come from fine clay and silt blanketing an originally uneven surface of ocean crust.

items.prompt: Fish that thrive in surface waters would struggle to live on an abyssal plain. What does the water there lack?
items.explain: Because oxygen is scarce, abyssal plains are inhospitable to organisms that would do well in the oxygen-rich waters above.

items.prompt: Geologists find very few ancient abyssal plains preserved in old rock layers. Why?
items.explain: Abyssal plains tend to be consumed by subduction, so they are poorly preserved in the sedimentary record.

items.prompt: Much of the mud on abyssal plains starts at the edges of the continents. How does most of it reach the deep floor?

options.label: Glaciers push it along the seabed
Turbidity currents carry it down canyons
Lava flows sweep it out to sea

items.explain: Much of the sediment is deposited by turbidity currents channelled from continental margins along submarine canyons into deeper water.

items.prompt: A biologist wants to predict what kind of animal community lives on a patch of abyssal plain. What should she measure first?

options.label: How much food sinks down and what it is
How much sunlight reaches the bottom
How tall the waves are at the surface
How far away the nearest island is

items.explain: The structure of abyssal ecosystems is strongly shaped by how fast food falls to the seafloor and what that settling material is made of.

pack.title: The Flattest Places on Earth
pack.question: How did so much of the deep ocean floor end up flat and smooth?

beats.title: The Flattest Places on Earth
beats.hook: More than half of Earth's surface is a dark, flat plain that was not recognized as its own feature until the late 1940s.

beats.prompt: Put the making of an abyssal plain in order.

items.label: Magma rises toward the mid-ocean ridge
It reaches the surface and forms new ocean crust
Seafloor spreading pulls the crust sideways
Fine clay and silt blanket the uneven crust

beats.explain: New crust forms where magma reaches the surface at mid-ocean ridges and is pulled sideways by spreading; sediment then blankets its uneven surface to make the plain.

beats.prompt: An animal used to oxygen-rich surface water is carried down to an abyssal plain. What problem does it face?
beats.explain: Oxygen is scarce on abyssal plains, which makes them inhospitable to organisms suited to the oxygen-rich waters above.

paragraphs.heading: Wide, flat and deep
paragraphs.text: Abyssal plains are flat plains on the deep ocean floor, usually found between 3,000 and 6,000 metres down. They generally stretch from the base of a continental rise out to a mid-ocean ridge. Taken together, they cover more than 50% of the Earth's surface. With the raised mid-ocean ridge and the abyssal hills beside it, they are one of the key parts of an ocean basin.

paragraphs.heading: Below the reach of sunlight
paragraphs.text: The ocean can be split into zones by depth and by whether sunlight reaches them. The top layer, the photic zone, is the lit part; its upper portion, the euphotic zone, has enough light for phytoplankton and plants to photosynthesize. In the clearest water the euphotic zone may reach about 150 m. Under the photic zone, the aphotic zone runs all the way to the seabed in permanent darkness. Because the ocean averages about 4,300 m deep, the lit layer is only a tiny fraction of its volume.

paragraphs.heading: Layers of the dark
paragraphs.text: The dark aphotic zone is itself divided into three regions by depth and temperature. First comes the bathyal zone, from 1,000 to 3,000 m, where the water cools from 12 °C to 4 °C as you go down. Next is the abyssal zone, from 3,000 to 6,000 m. That is the same range of depths where abyssal plains are usually found.

paragraphs.heading: Food falling from above
paragraphs.text: Nearly all ocean life depends on phytoplankton and other marine plants using photosynthesis to turn carbon dioxide into organic carbon, and that process needs energy from sunlight. Nearly all of this primary production happens in the photic zone. Creatures of the dark zone often swim upward to feed there. Otherwise they depend on material sinking from above, or on another energy source, as chemosynthetic archaea do near hydrothermal vents and cold seeps. On abyssal plains, the shape of each ecosystem depends strongly on how fast food reaches the floor and what that settling material is made of.

paragraphs.heading: Why the plains matter
paragraphs.text: Partly because they are so vast, abyssal plains are thought to be major stores of biodiversity. They also have a strong effect on how carbon cycles through the ocean, on how calcium carbonate dissolves, and on carbon dioxide in the air over a hundred to a thousand years. Deep sea coral reefs are mainly found 3,000 meters down and deeper, in the abyssal and hadal zones.

paragraphs.heading: Still barely explored
paragraphs.text: Nobody treated abyssal plains as a separate kind of seafloor feature until the late 1940s. Systematic study of any of them is recent. They stay poorly explored because they are dark and because the water pressure there can climb to about 750 times atmospheric pressure (76 megapascal). They also leave little trace in the rock record, because the process of subduction tends to consume them.
